definition: Enervate means to weaken or drain of energy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word enervate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know enervate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three straight hours of fluorescent-lit budget meetings enervated the new hire more thoroughly than any workout ever had.
Tire is ordinary and honest — a long walk tires you; it stops well short of enervate's deep draining.
Prostrate goes further than enervate — an enervated intern drags through the afternoon; a prostrated one is flat on the cot in the break room.

To sap is to bleed strength away little by little, the way a slow leak empties a reservoir over weeks. Enervate need not be gradual — one gray season of waiting can enervate a whole household — and it names the drained slackness left behind, not the leak itself.

To exhaust is to use energy up through honest effort — a race, a climb, a double shift — so the emptiness is earned. Enervate empties you without any work being done: tedium, grief, or thin air simply pulls the strength out while you sit still.

Drain is the plain, everyday word for emptying someone's energy, at home in any casual sentence. Enervate is the formal, exam-flavored counterpart and adds a shade the plain word lacks: the weak, slack, cut-sinew feeling left behind once the vitality has gone.

The e- is the 'out' prefix, and nerv- is Latin nervus, 'sinew': to enervate is, literally, to cut the sinews out.

Above all, never use it to mean energize — its unit-mate and mirror image — and expect the SAT to tempt you with exactly that swap.
Nearby sits emaciated, which is bodily wasting; enervation is spent energy, not lost flesh.
